theme: Anchor Your Event Schedule with Buffer Time

linkedin.text:
Here's a scheduling truth most event briefs ignore:

Back-to-back programming is a risk, not an asset.

Every senior leader I've spoken to remembers the conference where a keynote ran 20 minutes over and the rest of the day never recovered. Lunch was rushed. The afternoon panel started late. The gala dinner felt chaotic before it began.

What fixed it wasn't a better AV team or a stricter MC. It was whitespace in the schedule.

After producing 1,500+ events across 130+ destinations, the pattern is consistent: programs that feel polished to participants are built on schedules that have 10–15 minutes of genuine buffer between every major transition — not just a theoretical gap, but protected time that no one is allowed to colonize with 'just one more slide.'

If you're finalizing a conference or convention agenda and want a peer perspective on where the structural risks are, I'm glad to take a look. Drop a comment or send a DM.

Here's our rule after producing 1,500+ corporate events: every major block needs 10–15 minutes of intentional transition time. Not optional. Not negotiable.

The programs that feel seamless to your attendees? They're the ones where the schedule has room to breathe.

facebook.text:
One scheduling mistake we see again and again in corporate events: back-to-back sessions with zero breathing room.

When a keynote runs long (and it will), the whole day cascades. Catering goes cold. Breakout rooms fill before speakers are ready. Attendees arrive frazzled instead of focused.

The fix is unglamorous but effective: build 10–15 minutes of buffer between every major block. Not just after lunch — between every transition.

After 1,500+ events across 130+ destinations, we can tell you: the programs that feel effortless to participants are the ones with the most deliberate slack built in behind the scenes.
